section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: Colonists in the Western Hemisphere turned to enslaved African labor chiefly because
options: A. The region had few inhabitants when Spaniards arrived
B. Native workers lacked knowledge of sugar cultivation techniques
C. Aztec and Inca rulers had already established the slave trade
D. Sugar harvesting demanded far more workers than were available
items.explanation: Colonists turned to enslaved African labor because sugar — the Americas' great money crop — required enormous gangs of workers for planting, cutting, and milling, far more than the available European or Native workforce could supply. Native populations had been devastated by disease, and Europeans would not do the killing labor in sufficient numbers. The plantation system's insatiable demand for workers drove the turn to Africa.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The hemisphere was well populated; disease, not emptiness, created the labor shortage.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Knowledge of sugar techniques was not the issue; the sheer demand for workers was.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Aztec and Inca rulers did not establish the transatlantic slave trade; Europeans created it.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Sugar harvesting demanded far more workers than were available, driving the turn to enslaved African labor.

items.stem: The conquest Prescott described was facilitated most decisively by which of the following?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Florentine Codex, Book 12, c.1585; pre-1930
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following excerpt.

The historian portrays Cortés as a daring and resourceful commander whose small Spanish force toppled the Aztec Empire through bold leadership, shrewd alliances with peoples subject to the Aztecs, and superior weaponry — while also recording the cruelty of the conquest.
—After William H. Prescott, History of the Conquest of Mexico, 1843 (paraphrased)

options: A. Spanish naval supremacy, Pacific bases, and maritime supply lines
B. Aztec alliances with the Portuguese and other European powers
C. Cortés's conversion to Protestantism and religious reforms
D. Epidemic disease, Indigenous allies, and Spanish weapons
items.explanation: Prescott's conquest was facilitated most decisively by three forces: epidemic disease — smallpox ravaged Tenochtitlan, killing the emperor and demoralizing defenders; Indigenous allies — tens of thousands of Tlaxcalans and others who hated Aztec rule; and Spanish steel, horses, and firearms. Without disease and allies, a few hundred Spaniards could never have toppled an empire.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Spanish naval supremacy and Pacific bases were irrelevant to the land conquest of Mexico.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Aztecs allied with no European powers; their allies were Indigenous peoples who turned against them.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Cortés did not convert to Protestantism; he was a Catholic conquistador.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Epidemic disease, Indigenous allies, and Spanish weapons most decisively facilitated the conquest.

items.stem: A historian critical of Prescott's account would most likely argue that it

stimulus.text:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following excerpt.

The historian portrays Cortés as a daring and resourceful commander whose small Spanish force toppled the Aztec Empire through bold leadership, shrewd alliances with peoples subject to the Aztecs, and superior weaponry — while also recording the cruelty of the conquest.
—After William H. Prescott, History of the Conquest of Mexico, 1843 (paraphrased)

options: A. Overstates the cruelty of the Spanish toward Indigenous peoples
B. Ignores the role of Cortés and his captains entirely
C. Understates the decisive roles of Indigenous allies and epidemic disease
D. Denies that the Spanish conquest of Mexico ever occurred
items.explanation: A historian critical of Prescott would argue that his heroic narrative gives Cortés and his men too much credit while understating the forces that really decided the outcome: the tens of thousands of Indigenous allies who did most of the fighting, and the smallpox epidemic that devastated Tenochtitlan. Prescott's great-man story minimizes the Native and microbial actors that made the conquest possible.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Prescott records the conquest's cruelty; critics do not accuse him of understating Spanish cruelty.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Prescott centers Cortés and his captains; ignoring them is the opposite of his approach.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Critics argue Prescott understates the decisive roles of Indigenous allies and epidemic disease.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Prescott does not deny the conquest occurred; he celebrates it.

items.stem: Which of the following groups would most likely support the principles expressed in the passage above?

stimulus.pd_rationale: William Halsall, 1882; pre-1930
stimulus.text_stimulus: “In the name of God, Amen. We, whose names are underwritten, the loyal subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James, by the Grace of God, of Great Britain, France, and Ireland King, Defender of the Faith, etc. Having undertaken for the Glory of God and advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honor of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the First Colony in the Northern Parts of Virginia, do by these presents, solemnly and mutually, in the presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic, for our better ordering and preservation and furtherance of the ends aforesaid; and by virtue hereof do enact, constitute, and frame such just and equal Laws, Ordinances, Acts, Constitutions and Offices from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the Colony, unto which we promise all due submission and obedience. In witness whereof we have hereunder subscribed our names at Cape Cod, the 11th of November, in the year of the reign of our Sovereign Lord King James, of England, France and Ireland the eighteenth, and of Scotland the fifty-fourth. Anno Domini 1620.” Source: William Bradford, Mayflower Compact , 1646

options: (A) A 1600s plantation owner
(B) A Separatist minister
(C) An English Catholic refugee
(D) A representative of the English monarch
items.explanation: The passage — presumably the Mayflower Compact or a similar covenant — expresses the Separatist principle of self-government by mutual agreement: believers forming a civil body politic by their own consent. A Separatist minister, who had led his congregation out of the Church of England to worship freely, would most support principles of voluntary covenant and congregational self-rule.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. A 1600s plantation owner depended on hierarchy and coercion, not voluntary covenant.
option_explanations.B: Correct. A Separatist minister would most support the passage's principles of covenant and self-government.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. An English Catholic refugee sought toleration under authority, not Separatist self-rule.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. A royal representative served the Crown's authority, not the people's covenant.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Spanish policy in the region in the decades after the events Josephe describes?
options: (A) Spanish authorities accommodated certain aspects of Pueblo culture in the late 1600s and 1700s.
(B) Spanish armies and disease completely eliminated the Pueblo population of the Southwest.
(C) Defeated by the rebels, Spain permanently abandoned all its territorial claims in North America by 1700.
(D) Spain and Britain allied to impose joint European control over the interior of North America.
items.explanation: After the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, Spain reconquered New Mexico in the 1690s — but the reconquest was gentler than the old regime. Spanish authorities accommodated certain aspects of Pueblo culture, tolerating traditional religious practices they had once violently suppressed, and eased the forced-labor demands. The lesson of 1680 was that accommodation, not coercion, would hold the province.

option_explanations.A: Correct. After the revolt, Spanish authorities accommodated certain aspects of Pueblo culture in the late 1600s and 1700s.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Pueblo peoples survived; they were not eliminated.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Spain reconquered New Mexico in the 1690s; it did not abandon North America.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Spain and Britain did not ally to control the interior; they remained rivals.

items.stem: The phrase 'civil Body Politick' in the Compact is most significant because it established Weir's 1843 painting above depicts the Pilgrims' departure — the voyagers who formed the 'civil Body Politick' of the Compact.

stimulus.pd_rationale: Robert W. Weir, 1843; pre-1930
stimulus.text_stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"We, whose names are underwritten, the Loyal Subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James... Having undertaken for the Glory of God, and Advancement of the Christian Faith, and the Honour of our King and Country, a Voyage to plant the first Colony in the northern Parts of Virginia; Do by these Presents, solemnly and mutually, in the Presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick, for our better Ordering and Preservation..."
—Mayflower Compact, 1620 (abridged)

options: A. Direct rule of the colony by the English crown
B. The colony's independence from England
C. Government resting on the consent of the colonists themselves
D. Voting rights for all inhabitants of the colony
items.explanation: The Mayflower Compact's civil Body Politick was revolutionary: the signers formed a government by their own mutual covenant, deriving authority from the consent of the colonists themselves rather than from a royal charter or divine right. That act of self-constitution — government resting on the people's agreement — is the phrase's significance and the seed of American democratic theory.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Compact created self-government, not direct rule by the Crown.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The colonists still professed loyalty to the king; the Compact did not declare independence.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The civil Body Politick established government resting on the consent of the colonists themselves.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Compact did not grant voting rights to all inhabitants; it was signed by adult men.

items.stem: Josephe's testimony indicates that the Pueblo rebels' motives centered most directly on which of the following?

stimulus.text: Asked what drove the rebels to renounce Spanish authority, Josephe — a Spanish-speaking Pueblo Indian questioned by colonial officials after the 1680 uprising — answered that the causes were the ill treatment they suffered: Spanish officials beat them, seized their property, and forced them to work without pay. Asked why the rebels burned churches and images, mocked sacred objects, and killed priests, Josephe said he had heard it stated that while besieging the Spanish villa the rebels shouted that the Spaniards' God was dead and that only their own gods lived. Their captains ordered that the names of Jesus and Mary never be spoken, and Josephe reported seeing new houses of native worship built where the people danced their traditional ceremonial dances. — paraphrased from the 1681 interrogation of Josephe

options: (A) A dispute among Pueblo leaders over who would govern once the Spanish were expelled.
(B) A desire to reopen the pre-contact trade routes that Spanish missions had closed off.
(C) Promises of military aid from English colonists on the Atlantic coast.
(D) Specific daily abuses of colonial rule: beatings, seizure of their property, and forced labor without pay.
items.explanation: Josephe's testimony is specific about what drove the 1680 uprising: Spanish officials beat the Pueblo people, seized their property, and forced them to work without pay. These were not abstract grievances but daily, physical abuses of colonial rule. The rebels' motives centered on the concrete suffering inflicted by Spanish officials — the beatings, thefts, and unpaid labor Josephe describes.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Leadership disputes among Pueblo leaders were not the motive Josephe describes.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Reopening trade routes was not the cause; daily abuses were.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. No English military aid figured in the Pueblo revolt.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The rebels' motives centered on specific daily abuses: beatings, seizure of property, and forced labor without pay.

items.stem: The sentiments expressed by Washington in his Farewell Address most warn against partisan divisions that occurred before which of the following conflicts?

stimulus.text: “…Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally. “There is an opinion that parties in free countries are useful checks upon the administration of government, and serve to keep alive the spirit of liberty. This within certain limits is probably true; and in governments of a monarchical cast patriotism may look with indulgence, if not with favor, upon the spirit of party. But in those of the popular character, in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged. From their natural tendency it is certain there will always be enough of that spirit for every salutary purpose; and there being constant danger of excess, the effort ought to be by force of public opinion to mitigate and assuage it. A fire not to be quenched, it demands a uniform vigilance to prevent its bursting into a flame, lest, instead of warming, it should consume.” Source: President George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796

options: (A) The War of 1812
(B) The Civil War
(C) The Nullification Crisis of 1832
(D) The Korean War
items.explanation: Washington's Farewell Address (1796) warned that the spirit of party would tear the republic apart — and the partisan divisions he feared, between Federalists and Democratic-Republicans, raged in the years immediately before the War of 1812. The war itself deepened those divisions to the breaking point at the Hartford Convention. Washington's warning was aimed at the partisanship of the early republic, which the War of 1812 then tested.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Washington warned against the partisan divisions that occurred before the War of 1812.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Civil War came 65 years after the address; its partisanship was a different crisis.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Nullification Crisis was an 1830s sectional dispute, not the partisan division Washington addressed.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Korean War was a twentieth-century conflict, far beyond the address's horizon.

items.stem: The Royal Proclamation of 1763 most directly contributed to which of the following?

stimulus.image_caption: British colonies in North America, 1763-1776, from Shepherd's Historical Atlas (c. 1911), showing the Proclamation boundary.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Shepherd's Historical Atlas, c.1911; pre-1930

options: (A) It united British colonists and Native peoples in shared suspicion of London's imperial motives.
(B) It sharply reduced the flow of British immigrants to North America.
(C) It heightened military tensions between Britain and France in North America.
(D) It angered colonists, who saw it as an unjust restriction imposed by a distant government.
items.explanation: The Royal Proclamation of 1763 drew a line at the Appalachians and told colonists they could not settle beyond it. To colonists who had just fought a war they believed entitled them to western lands, the proclamation felt like an unjust restriction imposed by a distant government that neither understood nor cared about their ambitions. It angered them precisely because it blocked their future.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The proclamation angered colonists; it did not unite them with Native peoples.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. British immigration was not sharply reduced by the proclamation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The proclamation followed Britain's victory over France; it did not heighten Anglo-French tensions.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The proclamation angered colonists as an unjust restriction by a distant government.

items.stem: Grenville answered Franklin's demand for colonial representation in Parliament by arguing that
options: (A) Parliament already represented all the king's subjects through virtual representation.
(B) The Stamp Act would be only the first of many internal taxes the colonies would have to pay.
(C) No subject of the king possessed any right to question Parliament's authority.
(D) Refusing parliamentary taxes amounted to treason against the crown.
items.explanation: When Franklin demanded colonial representation in Parliament, George Grenville answered with the doctrine of virtual representation: Parliament already represented all the king's subjects, whether they voted for members or not, just as it represented Britons who couldn't vote. The colonists needed no actual seats because they were virtually represented. Americans found the doctrine absurd; Parliament found it sufficient.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Grenville argued Parliament already represented all subjects through virtual representation.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Grenville did not promise more internal taxes; he defended the one at issue.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Grenville's argument was about representation, not about forbidding all questions of authority.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Grenville did not call tax refusal treason; he called it unnecessary given virtual representation.

items.stem: The sentiments expressed in the image above were most reflected in which of the following in the latter part of the 1700s?

stimulus.image_caption: Benjamin Franklin, 'Join, or Die,' Pennsylvania Gazette, May 9, 1754.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Benjamin Franklin, 1754; pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: The image above: Franklin's 'Join, or Die' cartoon of May 9, 1754.

options: (A) The ratification of the Constitution
(B) The adoption of the Articles of Confederation
(C) The terms of the Treaty of Paris of 1783
(D) The publication of the Antifederalist papers
items.explanation: The image's sentiments — presumably celebrating the new nation's republican achievement — were most reflected in the ratification of the Constitution (1787–1788), the act by which the American people created their republican government. The Constitution's adoption was the era's great expression of self-government realized. The image belongs to the founding moment the Constitution embodies.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The image's sentiments were most reflected in the ratification of the Constitution.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Articles of Confederation were the earlier, weaker frame the Constitution replaced.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Treaty of Paris ended the war; the Constitution built the republic.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Antifederalist papers opposed the Constitution rather than reflecting its spirit.

items.stem: Logan's reference to Colonel Cresap suggests that

stimulus.text:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following excerpt.

"I appeal to any white man to say if ever he entered Logan's cabin hungry and he gave him not meat... During the course of the last long and bloody war Logan remained idle in his cabin, an advocate for peace... I had even thought to have lived with you but for the injuries of one man. Colonel Cresap, the last spring, in cold blood and unprovoked, murdered all the relations of Logan... There runs not a drop of my blood in the veins of any living creature. This called on me for revenge. I have sought it. I have killed many... But do not harbor a thought that mine is the joy of fear. Logan never felt fear."
—Logan (Tah-gah-jute), speech recorded 1774 (abridged)

options: A. Personal grievances and unprovoked settler violence fueled retaliatory raids
B. Logan sought British military aid and protection against the colonists
C. Logan had converted to Christianity and joined a mission church
D. The Iroquois Confederacy controlled the Ohio Valley and its trade
items.explanation: Logan names Colonel Cresap as the man whose unprovoked murder of Logan's family drove him to revenge — the speech's turning point from peace advocacy to retaliation. The reference shows how the frontier war worked: not through grand strategy but through personal grievances, as unprovoked settler violence against Native families ignited cycles of retaliatory raids.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Logan's reference shows personal grievances and unprovoked settler violence fueled retaliatory raids.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Logan did not seek British aid; he sought revenge on his own.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Logan had not converted to Christianity or joined a mission.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Iroquois Confederacy did not control the Ohio Valley; the conflict was local and personal.

items.stem: The image above was designed to unite the colonies in response to

stimulus.image_caption: Benjamin Franklin, 'Join, or Die,' Pennsylvania Gazette, May 9, 1754.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Benjamin Franklin, 1754; pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: The image above (replacing the bare title reference): Franklin's 'Join, or Die' cartoon of May 9, 1754.

options: (A) rising anti-British sentiment over taxation without representation in Parliament
(B) conflicts over territorial rights with the French and Native Americans
(C) increased conflict over religious differences between the colonies
(D) an economic downturn resulting from the Seven Years’ War
items.explanation: The image — Franklin's Join, or Die snake cartoon of 1754 — was designed to unite the colonies against the French and their Native allies during the French and Indian War. Published to support the Albany Plan of Union, it warned that divided colonies would fall to French territorial ambitions. Its purpose was colonial unity against the French threat, not against Britain.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The cartoon predated the Revolution; it was not about taxation without representation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The image was designed to unite the colonies against French and Native American territorial threats.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Religious differences were not the cartoon's subject.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Seven Years' War downturn was not the cartoon's occasion; the French threat was.

items.stem: The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions
options: A. They endorsed the new federal Constitution
B. They claimed states could refuse to enforce unconstitutional federal laws
C. They defended Adams's Sedition Act
D. They attacked Hamilton's economic program
items.explanation: The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions of 1798–1799 — Jefferson's and Madison's secret response to the Alien and Sedition Acts — claimed that states could refuse to enforce federal laws they deemed unconstitutional. The compact theory: the Constitution was an agreement among states, and the states could judge federal overreach. Interposition and nullification were born here.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Resolutions attacked federal overreach; they did not endorse the Constitution uncritically.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Resolutions claimed states could refuse to enforce unconstitutional federal laws.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Resolutions attacked the Sedition Act; they did not defend it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Hamilton's economic program was not the Resolutions' target; the Alien and Sedition Acts were.

items.stem: Democratic-Republican leaders answered measures like this one by
options: (A) calling on Congress to impeach President John Adams.
(B) challenging the laws before the Supreme Court.
(C) advancing state nullification of federal laws.
(D) boycotting the election of 1800.
items.explanation: Democratic-Republican leaders answered the Alien and Sedition Acts — the Federalist crackdown on dissent — by advancing the doctrine of state nullification: in the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, Jefferson and Madison argued states could interpose against unconstitutional federal laws. Nullification was the party's constitutional weapon against Federalist repression.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Democratic-Republicans did not seek Adams's impeachment; they sought electoral victory and nullification theory.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. They did not take the laws to the Supreme Court; they advanced state nullification.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Democratic-Republicans answered with state nullification of federal laws.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. They contested the election of 1800 vigorously; they did not boycott it.

items.stem: Which branch or level of government gave the Cherokee their strongest support in the 1830s?
options: (A) President Andrew Jackson, who championed their land rights.
(B) The Supreme Court, which denied Georgia authority over Cherokee lands.
(C) The United States Congress, which blocked removal legislation.
(D) The Georgia legislature, which defended Cherokee sovereignty against removal.
items.explanation: In the 1830s, the Cherokee's strongest support came from the Supreme Court: in Worcester v. Georgia (1832), Chief Justice Marshall ruled that Georgia had no authority over Cherokee lands and that only the federal government could deal with the tribe. It was the law on the Cherokee's side. But President Jackson refused to enforce it, and Congress passed removal anyway — the Court's support proved powerless.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Jackson championed removal, not Cherokee land rights.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Supreme Court gave the Cherokee their strongest support, denying Georgia authority over their lands.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Congress passed the Indian Removal Act; it did not block removal.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Georgia legislature demanded Cherokee lands; it did not defend their sovereignty.

items.stem: Who would have been most likely to oppose Jackson's war on the Bank?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1836 (lithograph by Henry R. Robinson; Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the cartoon described below.

The 1836 cartoon 'General Jackson Slaying the Many Headed Monster' shows President Andrew Jackson, dressed as a soldier, raising a cane to strike a many-headed serpent. Each head wears a crown labeled with the name of a Bank director or ally, and the creature is labeled 'Bank of the United States.'

options: A. A southern planter
B. A western farmer
C. An urban laborer
D. A northern businessman
items.explanation: Jackson's war on the Second Bank of the United States threatened the credit system that Northern businessmen depended on: the Bank stabilized currency, financed commerce, and disciplined state banks. A Northern businessman — tied to trade, manufacturing, and sound money — would most oppose its destruction. Planters, farmers, and laborers cheered the Bank's fall; the business class mourned it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Southern planters generally supported Jackson's attack on the Bank.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Western farmers were Jackson's base and applauded the Bank War.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Urban laborers backed Jackson against the moneyed monopoly.
option_explanations.D: Correct. A Northern businessman, dependent on the Bank's credit and stability, would most oppose Jackson's war on it.

items.stem: Parkman's grave markers ('MARY ELLIS DIED') most directly testify to

stimulus.text:
Questions 25–28 refer to the following quotation.

"MARY ELLIS DIED MAY 7th, 1845 … Such tokens were of common occurrence … we saw close before us the emigrant caravan, with its heavy white wagons creeping on in their slow procession, and a large drove of cattle following behind. … The women were divided between regrets for the homes they had left and apprehension of the deserts and savages before them." —Francis Parkman, The Oregon Trail: Sketches of Prairie and Rocky-Mountain Life, 1849 (abridged)

options: A. Native American military victories
B. The success of wagon trains
C. Government hospitals on the trail
D. The high mortality of the overland trails
items.explanation: Parkman notes that grave markers like MARY ELLIS DIED were of common occurrence along the Oregon Trail — the landscape was dotted with the dead. Disease, accidents, and exhaustion killed thousands of overland migrants; the trail was a corridor of graves. The markers testify to the high mortality of the overland trails, not to their success.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The graves were migrants' deaths from disease and hardship, not Native military victories.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Common graves testify to suffering, not to the wagon trains' success.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. There were no government hospitals on the trail; migrants buried their own.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The grave markers testify to the high mortality of the overland trails.

items.stem: All of the following events can be understood as consequences of the policy illustrated above EXCEPT

stimulus.pd_rationale: U.S. National Park Service map (work of the U.S. federal government, public domain). PD tag confirmed on Commons file page (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) the Trail of Tears
(B) King Philip’s War
(C) Creek War of 1836
(D) the Battle of Little Big Horn
items.explanation: The policy illustrated — Indian removal and the reservation system — produced the Trail of Tears, the Creek War of 1836, and ultimately the Battle of Little Bighorn, all consequences of dispossessing Native peoples. King Philip's War (1675–1676) belongs to a different century and a different policy world: it was a New England colonial conflict, not a product of nineteenth-century removal.

option_explanations.A: This was a consequence, so it is not the answer. The Trail of Tears was removal's direct product.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. King Philip's War (1675) predated removal policy by a century and a half.
option_explanations.C: This was a consequence, so it is not the answer. The Creek War of 1836 grew from removal pressures.
option_explanations.D: This was a consequence, so it is not the answer. Little Bighorn grew from the reservation system's failures.

items.stem: The cartoon above was most likely created in response to Jackson’s policies regarding

stimulus.text: King Andrew the First , Unknown Artist, c. 1833

options: (A) indigenous sovereignty
(B) federal tariff rates
(C) national finances
(D) American expansionism
items.explanation: The King Andrew the First cartoon (c. 1833) — Jackson in royal robes trampling the Constitution — was created in response to his war on the Second Bank of the United States: the veto, the removal of deposits, the assertion of executive power over national finances. The cartoon's subject is Jackson's financial policy and the constitutional crisis it provoked.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Indigenous sovereignty was not the cartoon's subject; national finances were.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Tariff rates were the nullification issue, not the cartoon's target.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The cartoon responded to Jackson's policies regarding national finances — the Bank War.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Expansionism was not the cartoon's subject.

items.stem: The emigrant caravans Parkman saw were made possible most directly by

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1868 by Currier & Ives. Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 25–28 refer to the following quotation.

"MARY ELLIS DIED MAY 7th, 1845 … Such tokens were of common occurrence … we saw close before us the emigrant caravan, with its heavy white wagons creeping on in their slow procession, and a large drove of cattle following behind. … The women were divided between regrets for the homes they had left and apprehension of the deserts and savages before them." —Francis Parkman, The Oregon Trail: Sketches of Prairie and Rocky-Mountain Life, 1849 (abridged)

options: A. The transcontinental railroad
B. Government land policy and military protection of trails
C. Air conditioning
D. The Panama Canal
items.explanation: The emigrant caravans Parkman saw — the great wagon trains of the 1840s — were made possible by government action: federal land policy that promised free or cheap western land, and Army protection of the trails against Native resistance. Washington opened the West legally and guarded it militarily. The caravans rolled on government-made roads, metaphorically speaking.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The transcontinental railroad came decades later, in 1869.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Government land policy and military protection of trails made the caravans possible.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Air conditioning is an absurd anachronism for the 1840s.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Panama Canal opened in 1914, seventy years after Parkman's journey.

items.stem: Washington's Farewell Address outlook is most clearly visible in which later action?
options: (A) Monroe's enunciation of the Monroe Doctrine (1823).
(B) McKinley's decision for war with Spain (1898).
(C) Wilson's Fourteen Points (1918).
(D) Roosevelt's signing of the Lend-Lease Act aiding Britain in 1941.
items.explanation: Washington's Farewell Address warned against permanent foreign alliances and entangling commitments. The Monroe Doctrine (1823) — declaring the Americas closed to European colonization while pledging noninterference in Europe — embodied that outlook: hemispheric self-reliance without permanent alliances. Monroe's doctrine was Washington's foreign policy translated to the 1820s.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The Monroe Doctrine most clearly reflects Washington's Farewell Address outlook.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. McKinley's war with Spain was interventionist, not Washingtonian.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Wilson's Fourteen Points embraced international entanglement, the opposite of Washington's counsel.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Lend-Lease committed America to Britain's war — precisely the entanglement Washington warned against.

items.stem: Frederick Douglass was most influenced by which of the following social movements?
options: (A) First Great Awakening
(B) Second Great Awakening
(C) Manifest Destiny
(D) Popular Sovereignty
items.explanation: Frederick Douglass — the escaped slave who became abolitionism's great voice — was most influenced by the Second Great Awakening. The revival's moral urgency, its demand for immediate repentance, and its perfectionist crusades against sin gave abolitionism its religious fire. Douglass's moral absolutism about slavery was the Second Great Awakening's ethic applied to the nation's great sin.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The First Great Awakening was a century earlier, in the 1730s–1740s.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Second Great Awakening's moral urgency most influenced Douglass.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Manifest Destiny celebrated expansion, not abolition.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Popular sovereignty was a political doctrine about territories, not Douglass's moral inspiration.

items.stem: As an African American officeholder of his era, Bruce was almost certainly a

options: A. Democratic

The Republican Party was the party of Lincoln, emancipation, and Black suffrage; the Democrats were the party of the white South. A Black officeholder in Reconstruction Mississippi could only be a Republican.

option_explanations.B: Correct. As an African American officeholder of the Reconstruction era, Bruce was almost certainly a Republican.

option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Irish transformed the city's labor structure; they did not leave it unchanged.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The table does not show Irish dominance of union leadership.

option_explanations.B: Wrong. The American System was Clay's nationalist program, not Southern states'-rights doctrine.

items.stem: The Union military draft angered many Northerners because
options: A. It opened the army to Black soldiers
B. It swept Irish immigrants into uniform
C. It let the drafted hire substitutes or buy exemption
D. It required martial law to enforce
items.explanation: The Union draft angered Northerners because it was a rich man's law: a drafted man could hire a substitute to go in his place or buy an exemption for $300. Workingmen — especially Irish immigrants — saw their neighbors' sons marching off while the wealthy bought their way out. The draft's unfairness, not its existence, sparked the fury that exploded in the 1863 New York draft riots.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Black soldiers' service was not the source of draft anger.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Irish immigrants were swept into uniform, but the anger was about the system's unfairness.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The draft angered Northerners because the drafted could hire substitutes or buy exemption.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Martial law was not required to enforce the draft.

items.stem: Scott favored the blockade-and-Mississippi strategy because he believed it would

"We rely greatly on the sure operation of a complete blockade of the Atlantic and Gulf ports soon to commence. In connection with such a blockade we propose a powerful movement down the Mississippi to the Gulf... the effect would be to isolate the rebellious states and cut off their foreign trade."
—Gen. Winfield Scott, outlining the 'Anaconda Plan,' 1861 (abridged)

options: A. End the rebellion with less bloodshed than a direct invasion
B. Free the enslaved people immediately
C. Provoke European powers to intervene
D. Destroy the cities of the South
items.explanation: General Winfield Scott's Anaconda Plan — blockade the Confederacy's ports and seize the Mississippi — was designed to end the rebellion with less bloodshed than a direct invasion of the South. Scott, the old general, believed strangulation would force surrender without the slaughter of great battles. The plan's logic was humanitarian as well as strategic: squeeze, don't storm.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Scott believed the blockade-and-Mississippi strategy would end the rebellion with less bloodshed.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Emancipation was not Scott's aim in 1861; the plan was about winning the war cheaply.

items.stem: Foner's interpretation implies which of the following about the Emancipation Proclamation?

stimulus.text: Historian Eric Foner argues that Lincoln, though personally antislavery, was neither an abolitionist nor a Radical Republican. Lincoln separated his oft-stated personal wish that 'all men everywhere could be free' from his constitutional duties as legislator and president in a system that protected slavery as property; even after the Emancipation Proclamation he favored gradual abolition, and his racial views, while evolving during the war, never made him a principled egalitarian like Frederick Douglass or Charles Sumner. (Paraphrased from Eric Foner, The Fiery Trial, 2010.)

options: (A) It was a constrained wartime measure, not the act of a committed abolitionist.
(B) It was struck down as unconstitutional.
(C) It freed every enslaved person in the United States immediately.
(D) It eliminated racism in the Northern states.
items.explanation: Eric Foner's interpretation presents Lincoln as personally antislavery but constitutionally constrained — a president who separated his wish that all men could be free from his duties in a system protecting slavery as property. That implies the Emancipation Proclamation was a constrained wartime measure: a military necessity issued by a man who was not a committed abolitionist, not the triumphant act of a moral crusader.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Foner's view implies the proclamation was a constrained wartime measure, not an abolitionist's act.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The proclamation was never struck down as unconstitutional.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The proclamation freed slaves only in rebellious areas, not everyone immediately.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The proclamation did not eliminate Northern racism.

items.stem: Northern opponents of Abraham Lincoln viewed the policy described above as

After the reading we were told that we were all free, and could go when and where we pleased. My mother, who was standing by my side, leaned over and kissed her children, while tears of joy ran down her cheeks. She explained to us what it all meant, that this was the day for which she had been so long praying, but fearing that she would never live to see.” Source: Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery: An Autobiography , 1907

options: (A) a necessary step to end the Civil War
(B) an egregious attempt by the president to push unneeded social revolution
(C) a precursor to open rebellion by southern states over the nature of slavery
(D) an overly sympathetic gesture to the South
items.explanation: Northern opponents of Lincoln — Democrats and conservative Unionists — viewed the Emancipation Proclamation as an egregious attempt by the president to push unneeded social revolution. To them, Lincoln had exceeded his war powers to remake Southern society, turning a war for the Union into a crusade against slavery. The proclamation was, in their eyes, presidential overreach with revolutionary consequences.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Lincoln's Northern opponents did not see emancipation as necessary; they saw it as overreach.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Northern opponents viewed the proclamation as an egregious attempt to push unneeded social revolution.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Southern rebellion preceded the proclamation; it was not the proclamation's precursor.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The proclamation was anything but sympathetic to the South.

items.stem: Which of the following statements regarding social issues in the post-Civil War 19th century is true?
options: (A) African Americans struggled against discriminatory practices even though the case of Plessy v. Ferguson technically outlawed legal segregation.
(B) While African Americans and women achieved suffrage during this period, both groups were often kept from voting through various illegal means.
(C) Impoverished southerners, both Black and white, had greater opportunities for upward mobility than did their northern counterparts due to sharecropping and the crop lien system.
(D) The influx of immigrant factory workers and the development of mass transportation caused the middle class to largely flee the major cities.
items.explanation: In the post–Civil War nineteenth century, the great cities filled with immigrant factory workers while mass transportation — streetcars, subways, commuter rails — let the middle class flee to the suburbs. Urban America sorted itself by class: workers in tenements, the middle class in streetcar suburbs. The statement captures the era's defining urban transformation.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Plessy v. Ferguson permitted segregation; it did not outlaw it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Women did not achieve suffrage in this period, and Black voters were suppressed.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Sharecropping trapped Southerners in debt; it did not offer superior mobility.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Immigrant workers filled the cities while mass transit enabled middle-class flight to the suburbs.

items.stem: According to the passage, Standard Oil's dominance meant that

"The profits of the present Standard Oil Company are enormous. For five years the dividends have been averaging about forty-five million dollars a year... a sum which, if distributed among the thousands of stockholders, would make every one of them rich — and yet the company was built up by methods which have made it the most hated corporation in the country."
—Ida Tarbell, on Standard Oil, 1904 (abridged and paraphrased)

options: A. A handful of men controlled enormous revenues that had to be reinvested yearly
B. Oil prices fell steadily to benefit consumers
C. Independent competitors thrived alongside the trust
D. The company paid no dividends to its owners
items.explanation: The passage describes Standard Oil's dominance: a handful of men controlled enormous revenues that had to be reinvested yearly — the trust's scale was so vast that its profits themselves became a problem of management. Tarbell's point is the concentration: immense wealth in few hands, growing by its own momentum. Dominance meant unaccountable financial power.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Standard Oil's dominance meant a handful of men controlled enormous revenues requiring yearly reinvestment.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The passage does not claim oil prices fell to benefit consumers.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Independent competitors were crushed, not thriving.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The company paid enormous dividends; that was part of Tarbell's point.

items.stem: Twain's central objection to Philippine annexation was that it

stimulus.text:

"I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific... But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines."

options: A. it would cost the United States too much money
B. it would provoke a war with Japan

The war against Filipino independence fighters exposed the imperial project as conquest — and Twain would not bless conquest.

option_explanations.B: Wrong. War with Japan was not Twain's concern.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Twain's central objection was that annexation meant conquest and subjugation rather than liberation.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Immediate citizenship for Filipinos was never the issue; subjugation was.

options: A. A nationwide religious revival
B. The Cold War
C. The Great Depression's need for tax revenue and jobs
D. The achievement of woman suffrage

option_explanations.A: Wrong. No religious revival drove repeal; economics did.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Cold War came later and had nothing to do with repeal.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Depression's need for tax revenue and jobs drove Prohibition's repeal.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Woman suffrage (1920) was achieved a decade before repeal and did not cause it.

items.stem: Which of the following is true of the policy referenced above?

stimulus.text: “Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is declared to be illegal…. Every person who shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize, or combine or conspire with any other person or persons, to monopolize any part of the trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, shall be deemed guilty of a felony.” Source: Sherman Antitrust Act, 1890

options: (A) It represented a repudiation of midwestern state policies around trusts and monopolies.
(B) It had minimal effect on most industrial monopolies until the Progressive Era.
(C) It represented a significant victory for the organized labor movement.
(D) It dramatically reduced American economic growth at the turn of the century.
items.explanation: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 declared trusts and monopolies illegal — but for its first decade it was barely enforced against industrial combinations; it was used more often against labor unions. The law had minimal effect on most industrial monopolies until the Progressive Era, when Theodore Roosevelt revived it as a trust-busting weapon. The statute slept until the Progressives woke it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The act extended the midwestern states' antitrust impulse nationally; it did not repudiate them.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Sherman Act had minimal effect on industrial monopolies until the Progressive Era.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The act was used against unions more than for them in its early years.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The act did not dramatically reduce economic growth; it was barely enforced.

items.stem: The ideas expressed in the passage would be most supported by which of the following groups?

stimulus.text: “The conscience of the people, in a time of grave national problems, has called into being a new party, born of the nation’s sense of justice. We of the Progressive party here dedicate ourselves to the fulfillment of the duty laid upon us by our fathers to maintain the government of the people, by the people and for the people whose foundations they laid. We hold with Thomas Jefferson and Abraham Lincoln that the people are the masters of their Constitution, to fulfill its purposes and to safeguard it from those who, by perversion of its intent, would convert it into an instrument of injustice. In accordance with the needs of each generation the people must use their sovereign powers to establish and maintain equal opportunity and industrial justice, to secure which this Government was founded and without which no republic can endure. “This country belongs to the people who inhabit it. Its resources, its business, its institutions and its laws should be utilized, maintained or altered in whatever manner will best promote the general interest. It is time to set the public welfare in the first place.” Source: Progressive Party Platform, 1912 (public domain).

options: (A) Industrial railroad owners
(B) Immigrant factory workers
(C) Urban middle-class professionals
(D) Rural tenant farmers
items.explanation: The 1912 Progressive platform — the people are the masters of their Constitution, resources and laws should serve the general interest, public welfare first — spoke to urban middle-class professionals: the lawyers, doctors, teachers, and reformers who filled the Progressive movement. They were the conscience-driven bourgeoisie who believed expertise and activism could clean up industrial America. The platform is their creed.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Railroad owners were the platform's targets, not its supporters.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Immigrant factory workers were not the Progressive platform's core constituency.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Progressive ideas would be most supported by urban middle-class professionals.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Rural tenant farmers were the Populists' base, not the Progressives'.

items.stem: During World War I, the propaganda effort headed by the Committee on Public Information used all of the following techniques to build public support for the war EXCEPT

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1917 poster by James Montgomery Flagg (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons; LOC print.

(B) mandating a sugar ration of one pound per week
(C) producing prowar posters, buttons, short films, and other media

What it did not do was mandate a sugar ration of one pound per week — rationing was the Food Administration's business under Hoover, not the propaganda committee's. The CPI sold the war; it did not ration sugar.

option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Sugar rationing was not a CPI propaganda technique.
option_explanations.C: The CPI did use this technique, so it is not the answer. Posters, buttons, and films were its stock in trade.
option_explanations.D: The CPI did use this technique, so it is not the answer. The Four-Minute Men spoke at public gatherings.

items.stem: [Image description: cartoon from The Masses, September 1915. Postal Inspector Anthony Comstock declares to a judge, 'Your Honor, this woman gave birth to a naked child.'] The cartoon's point is which of the following?

items.stem: Roosevelt's 1940 warning proved prescient when the nation later confronted

stimulus.text:
Questions 53–55 refer to the following quotation.

In a March 14, 1940 address to the American Civil Liberties Union, Eleanor Roosevelt said that traveling the country had made her conscious of the importance of civil liberties, warned that democracy is endangered whenever the light of liberty grows dim, and argued that while wartime nations lose freedoms of press, speech, and assembly, Americans at peace had a grave responsibility to guard them. —Paraphrase of Eleanor Roosevelt, address to the ACLU, Chicago, March 14, 1940 (abridged)

options: A. The Teapot Dome scandal
B. The Whiskey Ring scandal
C. Loyalty-security programs of the Second Red Scare
D. The Freedmen's Bureau
items.explanation: Eleanor Roosevelt warned in 1940 that even nations at peace must guard civil liberties, lest the light of liberty grow dim. Her warning proved prescient when the Second Red Scare's loyalty-security programs — loyalty oaths, blacklists, HUAC investigations — dimmed those very liberties in the late 1940s and 1950s. Peacetime America did exactly what she feared: traded freedom for security.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Teapot Dome was a 1920s corruption scandal, not a civil-liberties crisis.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Whiskey Ring was a 1870s scandal, unrelated to Roosevelt's warning.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Roosevelt's warning proved prescient with the Second Red Scare's loyalty-security programs.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Freedmen's Bureau was a Reconstruction agency, not a threat to civil liberties.

items.stem: The ad's emphasis on yearly new models reflects

stimulus.text:
Questions 25–28 refer to the following advertisement.

[A 1950s Ford automobile advertisement shows a smiling suburban family loading luggage into a gleaming new car parked before their ranch house; the copy celebrates annual model changes and easy credit terms.]

options: A. Government regulation of automobile design
B. Planned obsolescence and style-driven marketing
C. A postwar shortage of steel
D. Declining consumer purchasing power
items.explanation: The 1950s Ford ad's celebration of yearly new models — with easy credit to buy them — reflects planned obsolescence and style-driven marketing: Detroit's strategy of making last year's car feel outdated so consumers would buy again. The annual model change was not about engineering; it was about selling. Style, not substance, drove the postwar auto market.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Government did not regulate auto design in the 1950s; the market did.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The ad reflects planned obsolescence and style-driven marketing.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. There was no postwar steel shortage constraining auto production.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Consumer purchasing power was rising, not declining, in the 1950s.

items.stem: Kennedy's rhetoric of national purpose was aimed most directly at

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov-POTUS}}: official White House photograph, a work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

President Kennedy declared that just as earlier generations had ridden the first waves of industrial revolution and invention, his generation must conquer the new frontiers of science and space.
—After President John F. Kennedy, 'New Frontier' speech, 1960

options: A. Calming public fears of nuclear war
B. Defending racial segregation
C. Promoting across-the-board tax cuts
D. Rallying Americans behind an activist agenda in science and public life
items.explanation: Kennedy's rhetoric of national purpose — the New Frontier's call to conquer new frontiers of science and service — was aimed most directly at rallying Americans behind an activist agenda in science and public life. The moon shot, the Peace Corps, the call to ask what you can do: Kennedy wanted a generation mobilized for national greatness. His rhetoric was a summons to action, not a calming of fears.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Kennedy did not aim to calm nuclear fears; he aimed to mobilize national energy.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Kennedy did not defend segregation; his administration moved toward civil rights.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Tax cuts were later Kennedy policy, but the rhetoric's target was national mobilization.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Kennedy's rhetoric aimed at rallying Americans behind an activist agenda in science and public life.

items.stem: Hoffman's drug-fueled, chaotic narration is most useful to historians as evidence of

stimulus.text:
Questions 41–44 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

Abbie Hoffman recalled storming the Pentagon in 1967 — leaping fences with fellow protesters in a theatrical, chaotic demonstration meant to dramatize opposition to the Vietnam War.
—After Abbie Hoffman, on the 1967 Pentagon march

options: A. The counterculture's deliberate rejection of conventional politics
B. Yippie military strategy
C. Mainstream Democratic platforms
D. Conservative support for the war
items.explanation: Abbie Hoffman's chaotic, drug-fueled account of the 1967 Pentagon march is most useful to historians as evidence of the counterculture's deliberate rejection of conventional politics. The Yippies didn't lobby or petition; they staged guerrilla theater, mocking the system's seriousness. Hoffman's narration embodies the countercultural conviction that the political game itself was corrupt and absurd.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Hoffman's narration evidences the counterculture's deliberate rejection of conventional politics.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Yippies had no real military strategy; their theater was symbolic.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Hoffman's account opposes mainstream Democratic politics, not exemplifies it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Hoffman opposed the war; his account does not evidence conservative support for it.

items.stem: Carmichael's 1966 call for Black Power marked a break with

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-NYWT}}: New York World-Telegram & Sun photograph; copyright not renewed. Public domain.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

We are now engaged in a psychological struggle over whether Black people have the right to define themselves — to use the words they choose, to assert pride in being Black, and to demand power rather than merely beg for inclusion.
—After Stokely Carmichael, Black Power speeches, 1966–67

options: A. Marcus Garvey's back-to-Africa movement
B. Booker T. Washington's accommodationism
C. The organized labor movement
D. The nonviolent, integrationist civil rights mainstream
items.explanation: Stokely Carmichael's 1966 call for Black Power marked a break with the nonviolent, integrationist civil rights mainstream — the movement of King's dream of Black and white together. Black Power asserted that Black people should define their own goals and build their own power, without seeking white approval or integration. The break was with the beloved community's integrationism.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Garvey's back-to-Africa movement was a separatist ancestor, not what Carmichael broke with.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Washington's accommodationism was an earlier philosophy, not the 1960s mainstream.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The organized labor movement was not the tradition Black Power broke with.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Black Power broke with the nonviolent, integrationist civil rights mainstream.

items.stem: The March on Washington most directly pressured President Kennedy to

stimulus.text:
Questions 25–28 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

King told the marchers not to 'wallow in the valley of despair,' declaring his dream that America would one day live out the true meaning of its creed — that all men are created equal.
—After Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., 'I Have a Dream,' 1963

options: A. Propose federal civil rights legislation
B. Escalate American involvement in Vietnam
C. Cut federal taxes
D. End the Cuban trade embargo
items.explanation: The 1963 March on Washington — 250,000 people demanding jobs and freedom, King's dream speech electrifying the nation — most directly pressured President Kennedy to propose federal civil rights legislation. The march made civil rights morally unavoidable; within a year Kennedy had sent a civil rights bill to Congress. Mass demonstration forced presidential action.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The March on Washington pressured Kennedy to propose federal civil rights legislation.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The march did not concern Vietnam escalation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Tax cuts were not the march's demand.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Cuban embargo was not the march's subject.

items.stem: Loyalty oaths, blacklists, and Alger Hiss are all associated with the

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov}}: work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.

options: (A) civil rights movement
(B) New Deal
(C) Red Scare
(D) Great Society
