option_explanations.C: Correct. Loyalty oaths, blacklists, and Hiss are associated with the Red Scare.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Great Society was Johnson's 1960s domestic program.

items.stem: McGovern's claim that the war 'was a struggle among groups of Vietnamese until we intervened' challenged which American justification?

stimulus.text:
Questions 29–32 refer to the following quotation.

In an April 25, 1967 speech, Senator George McGovern argued that the war had begun as a struggle among Vietnamese groups before American intervention, and charged that the United States seemed determined to save Vietnam from Ho Chi Minh even at the cost of destroying the country. —Paraphrase of George McGovern, "The Lessons of Vietnam," April 25, 1967 (abridged)

options: A. That Vietnam directly threatened the U.S. mainland
B. That America was defending South Vietnam from communist aggression
C. That Congress had formally declared war
D. That NATO obligations required intervention
items.explanation: Senator George McGovern argued that Vietnam had been a struggle among Vietnamese groups before America intervened — a civil war, not a communist invasion. That claim directly challenged the American justification that the United States was defending South Vietnam from communist aggression. If there was no aggression to defend against, the whole rationale for intervention collapsed.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. McGovern did not claim Vietnam threatened the U.S. mainland; he denied the aggression narrative.
option_explanations.B: Correct. McGovern challenged the justification that America was defending South Vietnam from communist aggression.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The absence of a formal declaration was a separate legal issue.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. NATO obligations were never the justification for Vietnam.

items.stem: Reagan's use of religious and moral language to define American purpose in the world most directly continued which earlier American tradition?

stimulus.text:
Questions 5–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

President Reagan urged Americans to pray for those living under totalitarian rule — but until they found freedom, he warned, the West must stay vigilant and strong against the Soviet threat.
—After President Ronald Reagan's 'evil empire' speech, 1983

options: A. The Monroe Doctrine's non-involvement in Europe
B. Manifest Destiny's providential mission
C. Dollar diplomacy's commercial expansion
D. The Open Door policy in China
items.explanation: Reagan's 1983 evil empire speech — calling the Soviet Union the focus of evil, urging prayer for the captive peoples — used religious and moral language to define America's Cold War purpose. That providential mission most directly continued Manifest Destiny's tradition: the nineteenth-century belief that America had a God-given mission to spread its principles. Reagan's moral crusade was Manifest Destiny's Cold War heir.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Monroe Doctrine counseled non-involvement in Europe; Reagan preached moral confrontation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Reagan's moral language continued Manifest Destiny's providential mission.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Dollar diplomacy was commercial, not moral-religious.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Open Door was about China trade, not providential mission.

items.stem: Bush's 'new world order' rhetoric was prompted most directly by

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov-POTUS}}: official White House photograph, a work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 53–55 refer to the following excerpt.

In a September 1990 address to Congress, President Bush argued that Iraq's invasion of Kuwait offered a chance to build 'a new world order' — in which nations would cooperate through the United Nations to deter aggression, pursue shared prosperity, and uphold the rule of law, with America leading a collective-security effort.
—After President George H. W. Bush, address to a joint session of Congress, September 1990 (paraphrased)

options: A. Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in August 1990
B. The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989
C. The Iranian Revolution of 1979
D. The Vietnam War and its aftermath
items.explanation: George H. W. Bush's new world order rhetoric — his vision of nations cooperating under law after the Cold War — was prompted most directly by Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in August 1990. The invasion was the test case: would the world tolerate aggression, or would a new order enforce the peace? Bush's phrase was born in the Gulf crisis.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Iraq's invasion of Kuwait prompted Bush's new world order rhetoric.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Berlin Wall's fall was background, but Kuwait was the direct prompt.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Iranian Revolution was 1979, a different crisis.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Vietnam's aftermath was decades past; Kuwait was the immediate cause.

items.stem: The COVID-19 pandemic most closely resembles
options: A. The Great Depression
B. The Spanish Flu of 1918
C. The Red Scare
D. The First Great Awakening
items.explanation: The COVID-19 pandemic most closely resembles the Spanish Flu of 1918: a novel respiratory virus sweeping the globe, killing millions, overwhelming hospitals, and disrupting daily life worldwide. Both pandemics forced societies into masks, closures, and mass death on a scale no other American crisis matches. The parallel is epidemiological and social, not economic or political.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Great Depression was an economic collapse, not a pandemic.
option_explanations.B: Correct. COVID-19 most closely resembles the Spanish Flu of 1918.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Red Scare was a political panic about communism.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The First Great Awakening was an eighteenth-century religious revival.

section_1b.directions: Section I, Part B — Short Answer: 3 questions, 40 minutes. Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (A, B, C); write your answers in complete sentences. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, Question 2 on a primary source, and Question 3 on a non-text source (map, chart, image, or diagram). This part counts for 20 percent of the exam score.

questions.stimulus_text: Convinced that the Revolution was the work of a few miscreants who had rallied an armed rabble to their cause, British leaders expected the revolutionaries to be intimidated. They believed the vast majority of Americans were loyal but cowed by Patriot terror tactics, and would rise up, drive out the rebels, and restore loyal government in each colony.
questions.attribution: Paraphrased from Jeremy Black, Crisis of Empire: Britain and America in the Eighteenth Century (2008).
parts: A. Briefly explain one point of view about the American Revolution that the author describes in the passage.
B. Briefly explain one piece of evidence from 1763 to 1800, not mentioned in the passage, that supports the point of view described.
C. Briefly explain one piece of evidence from 1763 to 1800, not mentioned in the passage, that refutes the point of view described.
exemplar: The author describes the British point of view: that most colonists were loyal to the Crown and that the Revolution was the work of a small radical minority terrorizing the majority into silence.

The Olive Branch Petition of 1775 supports this view - even after fighting began at Lexington and Concord, the Continental Congress still petitioned George III for reconciliation, showing reluctance to break with Britain.
Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776) refutes it - the pamphlet's enormous popular readership showed broad popular enthusiasm for independence, not a cowed loyal majority.

questions.stimulus_text: The master class has always declared the wars; the subject class has always fought the battles. The master class has had all to gain and nothing to lose, while the subject class has had nothing to gain and all to lose - especially their lives.
questions.attribution: Eugene V. Debs, speech at Canton, Ohio, June 16, 1918.
parts: A. Briefly describe Debs's argument about war in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE way the federal government responded to antiwar dissent like Debs's during World War I.
C. Briefly explain ONE Supreme Court decision that addressed wartime restrictions on speech.
exemplar: Debs argues that wars are class conflicts in disguise: wealthy elites who declare wars never fight them, while working-class people are conscripted to kill and die for interests that are not their own.
Debs was prosecuted under the Espionage Act of 1917 for this speech and sentenced to ten years in prison - the federal government's most prominent wartime suppression of antiwar dissent.
The Supreme Court upheld Debs's conviction in Debs v. United States (1919), ruling that antiwar speech creating a 'clear and present danger' to recruitment could be punished.

questions.stimulus_text: The timeline shows: 1803 — Louisiana Purchase, as Napoleon abandons his American empire; 1807 — Embargo Act halts American trade with Britain and France; 1812–1815 — War of 1812 with Britain; 1814 — Hartford Convention of anti-war Federalists; 1815 — Battle of New Orleans makes Andrew Jackson a hero.
parts: A. Briefly explain ONE example of how foreign wars influenced American policy in the period 1801–1815.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND example of that influence in the same period.
C. Briefly explain ONE consequence of the War of 1812.
exemplar: Napoleon's failure to crush the Haitian slave rebellion, combined with looming war against Britain, convinced him to sell Louisiana in 1803 — doubling the United States at a stroke.

Jefferson's 1807 Embargo Act, a response to British and French seizures of American ships during the Napoleonic Wars, devastated American commerce and showed how European wars dictated American policy.
The War of 1812 fostered American nationalism and economic independence: the war spurred domestic manufacturing, discredited the Federalists after Hartford, and ushered in the 'Era of Good Feelings.'

section_2a.directions: Section II, Part A — Document-Based Question: 1 question, 60 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period). The question is based on 7 documents. In your response you must develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, use at least 4 documents to support your argument, use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents, and for at least 2 documents explain how the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to your argument. This part counts for 25 percent of the exam score.

dbq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the United States foreign policy changed between 1914 and 1917.

documents.text:
The effect of the war upon the United States will depend upon what American citizens say and do. Every man who really loves America will act and speak in the true spirit of neutrality, which is the spirit of impartiality and fairness and friendliness to all concerned.

The people of the United States are drawn from many nations, and chiefly from the nations now at war. It is natural and inevitable that there should be the utmost variety of sympathy and desire among them with regard to the issues and circumstances of the conflict.

Such divisions amongst us would be fatal to our peace of mind and might seriously stand in the way of the proper performance of our duty as the one great nation at peace, the one people holding itself ready to play a part of impartial mediation and speak the counsels of peace and accommodation, not as a partisan, but as a friend.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: Woodrow Wilson, sitting president at the war's outbreak. Purpose: rally domestic unity behind neutrality and position the United States as an impartial mediator. Audience: Congress and the American public, especially immigrant groups. Argument relevance: establishes the official neutrality baseline against which later change can be measured.

documents.text:
Dear Mr. President:
[I] ask your permission to enter into some detail with regard to the neutrality question. But let me assure you beforehand that I interpret your inquiry as referring exclusively to the views which are expressed to me by American citizens who sympathize with the German cause or who are disturbed by the vehement hostility to Germany on the part of the American press. My remarks refer in no way to the views of official Germany....

First, all cables sent by and received by wire pass uncensored, while all wireless news is censored. This reacts against Germany, because England sends all her news by cable, whereas Germany alone uses the wireless....

Second, the policy of the administration with regard to the holding up, detaining and searching of Germans and Austrians from neutral and American vessels is a reversal of the American policy established in 1812. It has excited no end of bitterness.

Third, the United States permitted the violation by England of the Hague Convention and international law in connection with conditional and unconditional contraband.... By permitting this new interpretation the United States practically supports the starving out policy of the Allies [and seriously handicapping] Germany and Austria in their fight for existence....

Many of the complaints refer more to the unfriendly spirit than to the actual violation of the law. Here above all belongs the unlimited sale of ammunition to the belligerents....
documents.sourcing_note: Source: Hugo Munsterberg, Harvard University professor, letter to Woodrow Wilson. POV: German-American intellectual sympathetic to Germany. Purpose: complain that American neutrality in practice favors Britain. Audience: President Wilson. Argument relevance: shows neutrality was contested at home and functioned as pro-Allied in effect, evidence of change beneath the official stance.

documents.text: Paraphrased from Robert Lansing, War Memoirs (1935). Lansing recalled that Britain enforced its blockade of American ships bound for mainland Europe despite repeated U.S. protests. Neutral vessels were seized and sent to British ports for cargo inspection without examination at sea, and even ships eventually released were detained so long that port expenses and the lost use of the vessel consumed the owners’ profits.
documents.sourcing_note: Source: Robert Lansing, War Memoirs (1935); the author was acting secretary of state during the period described. POV: retrospective insider account. Purpose: memoir justifying the American position. Audience: general readers. Argument relevance: documents how the British blockade disrupted American trade, creating pressure that tilted the United States toward the Allies.

documents.text:
Dear Mr. Stone:
I have received your letter...referring to frequent complaints or charges made...that this Government has shown partiality to Great Britain, France, and Russia against Germany and Austria during the present war.... I will take them up...

(1) Freedom of communication by submarine cables versus censored communication by wireless.
The reason that wireless messages and cable messages require different treatment by a neutral government is as follows: Communications by wireless can not be interrupted by a belligerent. With a submarine cable it is otherwise.... A more important reason, however, at least from the point of view of a neutral government is that messages sent out from a wireless station in neutral territory may be received by belligerent warships on the high seas....

(4) Submission without protest to British violations of the rules regarding absolute and conditional contraband as laid down in the Hague conventions, the Declaration of London, and international law.
There is no Hague convention which deals with absolute or conditional contraband, and, as the Declaration of London is not in force, the rules of international law only apply.... The United States has made earnest representations to Great Britain in regard to the seizure and detention by the British authorities of all American ships....

(9) The United States has not interfered with the sale to Great Britain and her allies of arms, ammunition, horses, uniforms, and other munitions of war, although such sales prolong the conflict.
There is no power in the Executive to prevent the sale of ammunition to the belligerents. The duty of a neutral to restrict trade in munitions of war has never been imposed by international law....

(20) General unfriendly attitude of Government toward Germany and Austria. If any American citizens, partisans of Germany and Austria-Hungary, feel that this administration is acting in a way injurious to the cause of those countries, this feeling results from the fact that on the high seas the German and Austro-Hungarian naval power is thus far inferior to the British. It is the business of a belligerent operating on the high seas, not the duty of a neutral, to prevent contraband from reaching an enemy....

I am [etc.]
W.J. Bryan
documents.sourcing_note: Source: Secretary of State William Jennings Bryan, letter to the Chairman of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations. POV: administration official defending policy. Purpose: rebut charges of pro-British partiality point by point. Audience: Senate committee. Argument relevance: shows the administration's legalistic defense of neutrality even as trade overwhelmingly favored the Allies - continuity of rhetoric amid changing practice.

documents.text:
NOTICE!
TRAVELLERS intending to embark on the Atlantic voyage are reminded that a state of war exists between Germany and her allies; that the zone of her waters includes the waters adjacent to the British Isles; that, in accordance with formal notice given by the Imperial German Government, vessels flying the flag of Great Britain, or of any of her allies, are liable to destruction in those waters and that travellers sailing in the war zone on ships of Great Britain or her allies do so at their own risk.
IMPERIAL GERMAN EMBASSY
documents.sourcing_note: Source: New York Times notice placed by the German Embassy. POV: German government. Purpose: warn Americans off British ships, establishing legal cover days before the Lusitania sinking. Audience: American travelers. Argument relevance: shows German escalation that pushed the United States from mediation toward confrontation.

documents.text:
Q: Did the Lusitania have on board on said trip 5400 cases of ammunition? If so, to whom were they consigned?
A: The Lusitania had on board, on said trip, 5468 cases of ammunition. The Remington Arms-Union Metallic Cartridge Co. shipped 4200 cases of metallic cartridges, consigned to the Remington Arms Co., London, of which the ultimate consignee was the British Government. G. W. Sheldon & Co. shipped three lots of fuses of 6 cases each, and 1250 cases of shrapnel, consigned to the Deputy Director of Ammunition Stores, Woolwich, England.
documents.sourcing_note: Source: Report from the American Customs Inspector in New York (1915). POV: American official record. Purpose: factual inventory of the Lusitania's cargo. Audience: government. Argument relevance: proves American munitions shipments to Britain, undermining claims of impartial neutrality and showing how economic ties pulled the United States toward the Allies.

documents.text:
...I have deemed it my duty, therefore, to say to the Imperial German Government, that if it is still its purpose to prosecute relentless and indiscriminate warfare against vessels of commerce by the use of submarines, notwithstanding the now demonstrated impossibility of conducting that warfare in accordance with what the Government of the United States must consider the sacred and indisputable rules of international law and the universally recognized dictates of humanity, the Government of the United States is at last forced to the conclusion that there is but one course it can pursue; and that unless the Imperial German Government should now immediately declare and effect an abandonment of its present methods of warfare against passenger and freight carrying vessels, this Government can have no choice but to sever diplomatic relations with the Government of the German Empire altogether.

This decision I have arrived at with the keenest regret; the possibility of the action contemplated I am sure all thoughtful Americans will look forward to with unaffected reluctance. But we cannot forget that we are in some sort and by the force of circumstances the responsible spokesmen of the rights of humanity, and that we cannot remain silent while those rights seem in process of being swept utterly away in the maelstrom of this terrible war.
documents.sourcing_note: Source: Woodrow Wilson, speech to Congress (during the Sussex crisis). POV: president. Purpose: deliver an ultimatum to Germany and assert American neutral rights. Audience: Congress. Argument relevance: marks the shift from impartial mediation to coercive threats - the endpoint of the change from 1914 neutrality.
